summary: For ages 5–7, teach that a rainforest has four vertical layers from ground to sky — forest floor (dark, damp, rotting leaves), understory (shady small trees/shrubs), canopy (a thick leafy roof where most animals and fruit are), and emergent (the tallest trees poking into bright sun). The organising idea is the vertical light gradient: dark below, bright above, which explains why most life crowds the sunny canopy (the emergent top is brightest of all). Build the layers bottom-to-top as a climb, link each to its inhabitants, and set this layered picture up as the map for placing animals and plants in later topics. A labelled vertical cross-section is the primary vehicle; a climb/elevator animation and ordering/which-layer checks are useful companions, not the only way to teach this.
misconceptions: A rainforest is one flat green space — it is layered, with very different conditions from floor to top
It is bright on the forest floor — the canopy blocks most light, so the floor is dark
Most animals live on the ground — most live up in the sunny canopy
The layers are all the same — each has different light, plants and animals
The emergent layer is a type of animal — it is the topmost layer of the tallest trees

activities.title: Climb the four layers of a rainforest
steps: Look at a tall cross-section of rainforest that is dark at the bottom and bright at the top, labelled floor → understory → canopy → emergent

Explore each layer from the ground up: the shadowy forest floor (damp, rotting leaves, beetles), the understory (shady shrubs, a resting frog), the canopy (monkeys, toucans, hanging fruit — 'most animals live here, in the sunny roof'), and the emergent giants (a harpy eagle in full sun and wind)
Use a light control (e.g. a slider) to dim the floor and brighten the top, watching how light fades toward the ground
Answer out loud or via lift-the-flap: 'Where is it darkest?' and 'Where do most animals live?'
activities.insight: A rainforest is a four-storey vertical world where light decreases toward the ground; because light and food are up high, most animals live in the sunny canopy rather than on the dark floor.

activities.title: Ride up through the forest as the light changes
steps: Watch or imagine an elevator rising from the dark forest floor up through the understory, canopy and emergent layer, with light brightening as it climbs
As the lift passes each level, say which animals and plants appear and whether it is getting lighter or darker
Stop the climb at a chosen layer and describe its light, conditions and who lives there
activities.insight: Moving upward through the forest, the light climbs from dark floor to bright emergent top, which is why each layer is a different kind of home.

activities.title: Order the layers and match the inhabitants
steps: Put the four layers in order from ground to sky: forest floor, understory, canopy, emergent
Match each layer to a key feature (e.g. canopy = thick roof of leaves; floor = dark and damp with rotting leaves)
Decide which layer an animal belongs to (e.g. beetles that eat rotting leaves on the floor, monkeys and toucans in the canopy, a harpy eagle in the emergent layer) and say why
Answer: which layer gets the most sunshine and which the least, and where most animals live and why
activities.insight: Secure the layer order, each layer's defining feature, and the causal link that the canopy blocks light so the floor is dark while most life gathers in the sunny upper layers.

activities.title: Talk a friend up through the layers
steps: Pretend to be a guide and walk a partner (or an adult) up the rainforest from floor to emergent top, naming each layer in order
At each layer, describe the light, the plants and at least one animal that lives there
Explain in your own words why it is dark at the bottom and bright at the top, and why most animals live in the canopy
activities.insight: Explaining the climb aloud requires the learner to produce the order and the canopy-blocks-light reasoning themselves, not just recognise it.

checkQuestion: If you stood on the ground at the very bottom of a rainforest at midday, would it be bright and sunny or dark? Tell me which, and then tell me WHY it's like that down there.
checkAnswer: It would be dark (and damp) on the forest floor, even at midday, because the thick roof of treetops — the canopy — blocks most of the sunlight before it reaches the ground. The bright sunlight is up high at the top (the emergent and canopy layers), so most animals and plants live up there where the light and food are.
